steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on multimodal fact-checking of image-text misinformation that adds a step for detecting which pieces of retrieved evidence are actually relevant. Cover the background, our motivation, the proposed model and how we evaluate it, and the main findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Multimodal misinformation and image re-purposing
- From detection methods to evidence-based fact-checking, and their gaps
- Motivation: not all collected evidence is relevant
- Contributions: RED-DOT and its modules
- Variants, training and evaluation (OOD-CV)
- Key findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Multimodal misinformation
  - misinformation intensified with internet + social media (cite); many adverse outcomes (cite)
  - generative AI (LLMs, Stable Diffusion) -> convincing, hyper-realistic misinformation (cite)
  - decontextualization / image re-purposing still prevalent challenge (cite)
  - Fig. 1: legitimate image used for false narrative linking 5G to COVID-19 transmission; actually anti-surveillance protest in Hong Kong
- Detection and fact-checking so far
  - surge of research on automated multimodal misinformation detection (cite): datasets (cite), detection methods (cite)
  - image-text pair alone not always enough; need external information = evidence (cite)
  - evidence-based fact-checking: text-based first (cite), then Multimodal Fact-Checking (MFC) (cite)
  - some MFC works: evidence from fact-checked articles (cite) -> "leaked evidence", unrealistic: human fact-checker's work as input for "early" detection (cite)
  - NewsCLIPings+: evidence collected from web (cite), no leaked evidence, used in many studies (cite)
  - but these assume all web items relevant; only verdict prediction
- Motivation
  - simulate realistic scenario like fact-checkers' daily work: many items gathered, not all relevant to support/refute claim
  - challenge: distinguish relevant vs irrelevant evidence to help verdict prediction
- Contributions
  - add Relevant Evidence Detection (RED) step to MFC
  - RED-DOT (Relevant Evidence Detection Directed Transformer): "Evidence re-ranking", "Modality Fusion", "RED"
  - re-ranking: intra-modal similarity -> relevance order + hard negative "irrelevant" samples
  - fusion: element-wise operations between modalities to cross-check relation
  - feature extraction / re-ranking: CLIP ViT B/32 and L/14 (cite), ALBEF (cite), BLIP2 (cite)
  - RED: relevance of each item to image-text pair, use relevant ones for veracity
- Variants and evaluation
  - variants: architectures (single or dual stage), mechanisms (guided attention)
  - multi-task learning on NewsCLIPings+ (cite); evaluated on VERITE (cite), real-world multimodal misinformation
  - Out-Of-Distribution Cross-Validation (OOD-CV): pick models that generalize across algorithmic training data (NewsCLIPings+) and real-world data (VERITE)
- Findings (ablation + comparative experiments)
  - (1) OOD-CV finds better models than "In-Distribution Validation" (ID-V) (Section 4.1)
  - (2) with re-ranking, one evidence per modality enough; more adds noise, lowers performance
  - (3) combining element-wise ops boosts accuracy vs simple late-fusion concatenation
  - (4) beats methods without external evidence by up to 33.7%; RED-DOT -Baseline (no RED module) by 8.9%
  - beats state-of-the-art on NewsCLIPings+ by up to 3%, without multiple backbone encoders, numerous evidence, extra features

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Misinformation has spread much more in the digital age, with the internet and social media platforms, and it has many negative outcomes. Advances in generative AI, like Large Language Models and Stable Diffusion, can now be used to make misinformation that is convincing and hyper-realistic. Still, decontextualization or image re-purposing, where images are taken out of their original context to support false narratives, is still a common challenge in multimodal misinformation detection. For example, Fig. 1 shows a real-world case where a legitimate image is used as evidence for a false narrative that links 5G technology to the transmission of COVID-19, while in reality the image shows an anti-surveillance protest in Hong Kong.

In recent years there has been a lot more research attention on automated multimodal misinformation detection, with work on creating multimodal misinformation datasets and on detection methods. But analysing only an image-text pair is not always enough to detect misinformation. Very often it is necessary to bring in and cross-examine external information, i.e., evidence. For this reason researchers have looked at methods for automated, evidence-based fact-checking, first with text-based approaches and more recently with Multimodal Fact-Checking (MFC). Some MFC works collect the external evidence directly from fact-checked articles. This can be seen as “leaked evidence” and it creates an unrealistic scenario, where the work of a human fact-checker is used as input while trying to detect new emerging claims “early”. On the other hand, the NewsCLIPings+ dataset has external information collected from the web, so it does not have “leaked evidence”, and it has been used recently in many studies. However, these MFC works assumed that all the external items collected from the web were relevant, and they only dealt with the task of verdict prediction.

Motivation. We want to simulate a more realistic scenario, similar to what fact-checkers deal with every day, where many pieces of information are gathered and examined but not all of them are relevant for supporting or refuting a claim. So the challenge is to tell relevant and irrelevant evidence apart effectively, to help the overall verdict prediction.

- Contributions
  - add Relevant Evidence Detection (RED) step to MFC
  - RED-DOT (Relevant Evidence Detection Directed Transformer): "Evidence re-ranking", "Modality Fusion", "RED"
  - re-ranking: intra-modal similarity -> relevance order + hard negative "irrelevant" samples
  - fusion: element-wise operations between modalities to cross-check relation
  - feature extraction / re-ranking: CLIP ViT B/32 and L/14 (cite), ALBEF (cite), BLIP2 (cite)
  - RED: relevance of each item to image-text pair, use relevant ones for veracity

- Variants and evaluation
  - variants: architectures (single or dual stage), mechanisms (guided attention)
  - multi-task learning on NewsCLIPings+ (cite); evaluated on VERITE (cite), real-world multimodal misinformation
  - Out-Of-Distribution Cross-Validation (OOD-CV): pick models that generalize across algorithmic training data (NewsCLIPings+) and real-world data (VERITE)

- Findings (ablation + comparative experiments)
  - (1) OOD-CV finds better models than "In-Distribution Validation" (ID-V) (Section 4.1)
  - (2) with re-ranking, one evidence per modality enough; more adds noise, lowers performance
  - (3) combining element-wise ops boosts accuracy vs simple late-fusion concatenation
  - (4) beats methods without external evidence by up to 33.7%; RED-DOT -Baseline (no RED module) by 8.9%
  - beats state-of-the-art on NewsCLIPings+ by up to 3%, without multiple backbone encoders, numerous evidence, extra features

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Misinformation has spread much more in the digital age, with the internet and social media platforms, and it has many negative outcomes. Advances in generative AI, like Large Language Models and Stable Diffusion, can now be used to make misinformation that is convincing and hyper-realistic. Still, decontextualization or image re-purposing, where images are taken out of their original context to support false narratives, is still a common challenge in multimodal misinformation detection. For example, Fig. 1 shows a real-world case where a legitimate image is used as evidence for a false narrative that links 5G technology to the transmission of COVID-19, while in reality the image shows an anti-surveillance protest in Hong Kong.

In recent years there has been a lot more research attention on automated multimodal misinformation detection, with work on creating multimodal misinformation datasets and on detection methods. But analysing only an image-text pair is not always enough to detect misinformation. Very often it is necessary to bring in and cross-examine external information, i.e., evidence. For this reason researchers have looked at methods for automated, evidence-based fact-checking, first with text-based approaches and more recently with Multimodal Fact-Checking (MFC). Some MFC works collect the external evidence directly from fact-checked articles. This can be seen as “leaked evidence” and it creates an unrealistic scenario, where the work of a human fact-checker is used as input while trying to detect new emerging claims “early”. On the other hand, the NewsCLIPings+ dataset has external information collected from the web, so it does not have “leaked evidence”, and it has been used recently in many studies. However, these MFC works assumed that all the external items collected from the web were relevant, and they only dealt with the task of verdict prediction.

Motivation. We want to simulate a more realistic scenario, similar to what fact-checkers deal with every day, where many pieces of information are gathered and examined but not all of them are relevant for supporting or refuting a claim. So the challenge is to tell relevant and irrelevant evidence apart effectively, to help the overall verdict prediction.

Contributions. We add the step of Relevant Evidence Detection (RED) as part of the MFC process. Specifically, we propose the Relevant Evidence Detection Directed Transformer (RED-DOT), which has three modules: “Evidence re-ranking”, “Modality Fusion” and “RED”. “Evidence re-ranking” uses intra-modal similarity to re-rank the evidence by relevance and to create hard negative “irrelevant” samples. “Modality Fusion” uses element-wise operations between the two modalities to cross-check how they relate. For feature extraction and evidence re-ranking we try CLIP ViT B/32 and L/14, and also ALBEF and BLIP2. Last, “RED” looks at all the given pieces of information, decides if they are relevant to the image-text pair, and uses the relevant ones to judge whether the pair is true.

We explore many variants of RED-DOT, with different architectures (e.g., single or dual stage) and mechanisms (e.g., guided attention). RED-DOT is optimized with multi-task learning on the NewsCLIPings+ dataset, and we also evaluate it on the VERITE benchmark, which has real-world multimodal misinformation. Finally, we propose the Out-Of-Distribution Cross-Validation (OOD-CV) evaluation protocol, to pick models that generalize better across algorithmically created training data (NewsCLIPings+) and real-world data (VERITE).

Findings. We run extensive ablation and comparative experiments, and they show several key findings: (1) OOD-CV picks models that perform better than the usual “In-Distribution Validation” (ID-V) (See Section 4.1). (2) With evidence re-ranking, one piece of evidence per modality is enough, and more information can add noise and lower the overall performance. (3) Combining element-wise operations can boost detection accuracy a lot, especially compared to simple late-fusion concatenation. (4) RED-DOT beats prior methods that do not use external evidence by a large margin of up to 33.7%, and the RED-DOT -Baseline, which does not use the RED module, by 8.9%. Also, RED-DOT beats the current state-of-the-art on NewsCLIPings+ by up to 3% without needing multiple backbone encoders, lots of evidence or extra features.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The dissemination of misinformation has greatly intensified in the digital age with the arrival of the internet and social media platforms [1] and has numerous adverse outcomes [2,3,4,5,6,7]. Advances in generative AI, such as Large Language Models and Stable Diffusion, can now be exploited to create convincing and hyper-realistic misinformation [8,9]. Nevertheless, decontextualization or image re-purposing, where images are taken out of their original context to support false narratives, remains a prevalent challenge in multimodal misinformation detection [10,11]. For instance, Fig. 1 shows a real-world example where a legitimate image is used as evidence to promote a false narrative linking 5G technology to the transmission of COVID-19, when in reality the image captures an anti-surveillance protest in Hong Kong.

However, relying solely on the analysis of an image-text pair is not always sufficient for detecting misinformation. More often than not, incorporating and cross-examining external information, i.e., evidence, is necessary [24]. To this end, researchers have explored methods for automated, evidence-based fact-checking, initially focusing on text-based approaches [25,26,27,28] and, more recently, moving into Multimodal Fact-Checking (MFC) [29,30,31]. Some MFC works collect external evidence directly from fact-checked articles [29,30], which can be considered “leaked evidence” and introduces an unrealistic scenario: using the work of human fact-checkers as input while trying to “early” detect emerging new claims [32]. Conversely, the NewsCLIPings+ dataset, which comprises external information collected from the web [31], does not suffer from “leaked evidence” and has recently been used in numerous studies [31,33,34]. Nevertheless, these MFC works assumed that all external items collected from the web were relevant and addressed only the task of verdict prediction.

Motivation. We aim to simulate a more realistic scenario, akin to what fact-checkers face daily, where multiple pieces of information are gathered and examined, but not all of them are necessarily relevant for supporting or refuting a claim. The challenge therefore lies in effectively distinguishing between relevant and irrelevant evidence in order to support the overall verdict prediction process.

Contributions. We incorporate the step of Relevant Evidence Detection (RED) into the MFC process. Specifically, we propose the Relevant Evidence Detection Directed Transformer (RED-DOT), which comprises “Evidence re-ranking”, “Modality Fusion” and “RED” modules. “Evidence re-ranking” uses intra-modal similarity to re-rank the evidence by relevance and to create hard negative “irrelevant” samples. “Modality Fusion” applies element-wise operations between the two modalities in order to cross-check their relation. For feature extraction and evidence re-ranking we experiment with CLIP ViT B/32 and L/14 [35] as well as ALBEF [36] and BLIP2 [37]. Finally, “RED” examines all provided pieces of information, determines their relevance to the image-text pair and uses the relevant ones to assess the pair’s veracity.

We explore numerous variants of RED-DOT, with different architectures (e.g., single or dual stage) and mechanisms (e.g., guided attention). RED-DOT is optimized via multi-task learning on the NewsCLIPings+ dataset [31], and its performance is also evaluated on the VERITE benchmark [38], which comprises real-world multimodal misinformation. Finally, we propose the Out-Of-Distribution Cross-Validation (OOD-CV) evaluation protocol to capture models that generalize better across algorithmically created training data (NewsCLIPings+) and real-world data (VERITE).

Findings. Our extensive ablation and comparative experiments demonstrate several key findings: (1) OOD-CV captures models with better performance than conventional “In-Distribution Validation” (ID-V) (See Section 4.1). (2) With evidence re-ranking, a single piece of evidence per modality suffices, while additional information can introduce noise and decrease overall performance. (3) Combining element-wise operations can significantly boost detection accuracy, especially compared with simple late-fusion concatenation. (4) RED-DOT surpasses prior methods that do not incorporate external evidence by a substantial margin of up to 33.7%, and the RED-DOT -Baseline, which does not use the RED module, by 8.9%. Moreover, RED-DOT surpasses the current state-of-the-art on NewsCLIPings+ by up to 3% without requiring multiple backbone encoders, numerous pieces of evidence or additional features.
